headline: UK and EU agree youth scheme and food-trade deal at Brussels summit, but university fees are left unresolved

terms.meaning: A deal to align food and farming checks so goods can cross borders with less paperwork.
A scheme that puts a price on carbon pollution, which the UK and EU plan to link.
The number of people arriving to live in a country minus those leaving.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree youth scheme and food-trade deal at Brussels summit, but university fees are left unresolved
levels.body:
At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, the UK and the EU announced a package that includes a youth experience scheme and a common sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) area, aimed at easing trade in food and farm goods. Euronews described it as three deals, the third being an emissions trading link.

Under the youth scheme, 100,000 young people from each side a year could live in the other's territory for up to three years. Participants would be aged 18 to 31, with no access to benefits and no dependants. The deal is meant to apply no later than 2028, with opportunities open by January 2030 at the latest. The UK government says it is capped and time-limited and estimates it adds no more than 14,000 to annual net migration.

The SPS area is intended to ease goods trade between Great Britain and Northern Ireland and to make pet travel to the EU simpler. The SPS and emissions trading agreements still have to be concluded and brought into force. Cheaper university fees for EU students were not agreed, and both sides committed to settle that within six months.
levels.why: It is the most significant UK-EU trade and mobility agreement since Brexit and shapes everyday trade, travel and study.

levels.headline: UK and EU strike youth scheme and food-trade deal, with university fees still to be settled
levels.body:
The UK and the EU agreed a package of deals at a summit in Brussels on 20 November, including a youth experience scheme and a shared system of food and farming rules (an SPS area). 

Under the youth scheme, up to 100,000 people from each side a year, aged 18 to 31, could live in the other's territory for up to three years. They would not be able to claim benefits or bring dependants. The UK government says it would add no more than 14,000 a year to net migration.

The food and farming deal is meant to cut checks between Great Britain and Northern Ireland and make travelling with pets to the EU easier. The SPS and carbon agreements still have to be finalised and brought into force. Lower university fees for EU students were not agreed, and a decision is promised within six months.
levels.why: It changes how easily goods and young people can move between Britain and the EU.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU agree a youth scheme and a food-trade deal, but not lower university fees
levels.body:
Britain and the EU reached a set of agreements at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. They cover a youth scheme, easier trade in food and farm products, and a link between their systems for pricing carbon pollution.

The youth scheme would let up to 100,000 young people from each side live in the other's territory every year, for up to three years. They would be aged between 18 and 31, and could not claim benefits or bring family members. The UK government says it is capped and would add no more than 14,000 a year to net migration.

The food deal aims to reduce paperwork and checks, especially between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and to make taking pets to the EU simpler. Lower university fees for EU students were left for later, with both sides promising a deal within six months.
levels.why: It affects trade, travel and study for people on both sides of the Channel.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree new deals on young people and food trade
levels.body:
The UK and the European Union agreed several new deals at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. They cover a scheme for young people, simpler rules for trading food, and a link between their carbon pricing systems.

Under the youth scheme, 100,000 young people from the UK and 100,000 from the EU could each live in the other's area every year for up to three years. They would be aged 18 to 31 and could not claim benefits. The UK government says it would add no more than 14,000 a year to net migration, which is the number of people arriving minus those leaving.

The food deal should cut paperwork and checks, especially for goods moving between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It should also make it easier to take pets to the EU. A deal on cheaper university fees for EU students was not reached, but both sides promised to agree one within six months.
levels.why: These deals could make travelling, working, studying and buying food from Europe easier.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree deals on young people, food and pollution pricing
levels.body:
The UK and the EU have agreed some new deals after talks in Brussels on 20 November. One lets young people live and work in each other's countries for a time. Another makes it easier to trade food and farm products. A third links the way they put a price on carbon pollution.

Each year, 100,000 young people from the UK and 100,000 from the EU could take part. They would be aged 18 to 31 and could stay for up to three years. They could not claim benefits or bring family with them. The government says it would add no more than 14,000 a year to net migration, meaning the number of people moving in minus those moving out.

The food deal should mean fewer checks and less paperwork at borders. It should also make taking a pet to Europe simpler. Lower university fees for EU students were not agreed yet. Both sides say they will settle that within six months.
levels.why: It could make life easier for young people, shoppers and food businesses.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree to make it easier to work, study and trade food
levels.body:
The UK and the EU have agreed some new deals. They met in Brussels on 20 November. The deals are about young people, food, and the cost of pollution.

The first deal is a scheme for young people. Each year, 100,000 young people from the UK and 100,000 from the EU could go and live in the other place. They would be aged 18 to 31. They could stay for up to three years. They could not claim benefits or bring family. The government says it would add only a small number of people to the UK each year.

The second deal is about food. At the moment, food and farm goods face a lot of checks at borders. The new rules should mean fewer checks and less paperwork. Taking a pet abroad should also get simpler.

One thing was not agreed. This is cheaper university fees for students from the EU. Both sides say they will decide within six months.
levels.why: It could change who can live and study here, and what food costs and how easily it arrives.

levels.headline: UK and EU agree new deals on young people and food
levels.body:
The UK and the EU have made some new deals. Leaders met in Brussels on 20 November. Brussels is the city in Belgium where the EU is based.

One deal is for young people. Every year, 100,000 young people from the UK and 100,000 from the EU could live in each other's countries. They would be aged between 18 and 31. They could stay for up to three years. They could not get benefits or bring family with them. 

Another deal is about food. Right now, food going between the UK and the EU gets checked at borders. This takes time and costs money. The new deal should mean fewer checks. It should also make it easier to take pets on trips to Europe.

One thing is still to be decided. That is the price of university for students from the EU. Both sides say they will agree on it within six months.
levels.why: It may make travel, study and food trade between Britain and Europe easier.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU make new deals
levels.body:
The UK and the EU have made some new deals. The EU is a group of countries in Europe. The UK left the group in 2020, so now the two have to agree on how they work together.

On 20 November, leaders met in Belgium. They agreed that young people could live in each other's countries for a while. Each year, 100,000 people from each side could do this. They would be aged 18 to 31. They could stay up to three years.

They also agreed to make buying and selling food easier. Today, lorries carrying food have to stop for checks at borders. The new rules should mean fewer checks. That should save time and money.

Some things still need more work. One is the price of university for students from the EU. The leaders said they will decide that within six months. The first young people probably will not take part for a few years.
levels.why: These deals could make it easier for young people to live abroad and for food to cross borders.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe agree to work together more
levels.body:
Two big groups have made a deal. One is the UK, where we live. The other is the EU, a group of countries in Europe that work together. They met in a city called Brussels to talk.

They agreed that young people can go and live in each other's countries for a while. They could stay for up to three years. They could go to school or work there. This is not for a few years yet.

They also agreed to make it easier to send food across borders. Food is checked when it moves from one country to another. Now there should be fewer checks. That means less waiting. It should also help families who want to take pets on holiday.

There is one thing they have not decided. It is how much students from Europe pay to study here. They have said they will decide soon.
levels.why: It could make life easier for young people and families who travel.

levels.headline: Britain and Europe agree to be better friends
levels.body:
Imagine two neighbours who had a big argument a few years ago. They stopped sharing and stopped visiting each other. Now they have sat down to talk, and they have agreed to be friendlier.

Britain and the countries of Europe met in a city called Brussels. They agreed that some young people can live in each other's countries for a while. It is a bit like a long school exchange visit. You go to stay somewhere new, and you learn about it.

They also agreed to make it easier to send food from one place to another. Lorries carrying food will not have to wait as long at the borders. It is like a queue at the school canteen getting shorter.

There are still some things the neighbours need to talk about. They have promised to talk again soon.
levels.why: It shows Britain and Europe working together more, which can help people on both sides.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.25% at 7,182.78 on Wednesday as the Dow rises 0.33% and the Nasdaq falls 0.62%

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
An index dominated by technology firms.
An index of 30 large US companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.25% at 7,182.78 on Wednesday as the Dow rises 0.33% and the Nasdaq falls 0.62%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.25% at 7,182.78 on Wednesday 25 November, the last completed session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to 50,182.95, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% to 23,585.80.

The day was volatile. At their lows the Dow was down more than 1,100 points (2.2%), the Nasdaq 4.6% and the S&P 500 3.2%. The selling was led by shares linked to artificial intelligence. CNBC said part of the rebound reflected thin trading before the Thanksgiving holiday and a widely shared blog post by the investor Michael Burry.

Investors were also weighing new tariff proposals from the White House and a rise in the Fed's preferred inflation gauge to 3.8%. US markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut early, at 1pm Eastern, on Friday.
levels.why: Share prices reflect confidence about the economy and affect pensions and savings.

levels.headline: S&P 500 slips 0.25% to 7,182.78 as the Dow gains and the Nasdaq falls
levels.body:
The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 25 November down 0.25% at 7,182.78. The Dow rose 0.33% to 50,182.95, while the Nasdaq fell 0.62% to 23,585.80. This was the last completed trading session.

Shares swung widely during the day. The Dow was down more than 1,100 points at its worst, with the Nasdaq down 4.6% and the S&P 500 down 3.2%. Stocks tied to artificial intelligence led the selling. They recovered after a quiet, pre-holiday market and a widely shared blog post from the investor Michael Burry.

Traders were also considering fresh US tariff proposals and a rise in a key inflation measure to 3.8%. US markets are shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday.
levels.why: Big moves in US shares can affect investments and pensions around the world.

levels.headline: US stocks end mixed after a wild day: S&P 500 down 0.25%, Dow up 0.33%
levels.body:
US shares ended a wild Wednesday mixed. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big US companies, closed down 0.25% at 7,182.78. The Dow rose 0.33% to 50,182.95. The Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80.

Earlier the Dow had been down more than 1,100 points, and the Nasdaq had dropped 4.6%. Shares in companies linked to artificial intelligence were sold heavily. Prices then bounced back, helped by light trading before the Thanksgiving holiday and a blog post by the investor Michael Burry that was widely shared.

Investors were also thinking about new US tariff plans, and about inflation, the rise in prices, which is at 3.8% by a measure the US central bank likes. Markets are closed on Thursday.
levels.why: Falling or rising markets can change the value of savings and pensions.

levels.headline: US shares end mixed after a day of big swings
levels.body:
US shares ended mixed on Wednesday 25 November. The S&P 500, an index of 500 large companies, closed down 0.25% at 7,182.78. The Dow, an index of 30 big firms, rose 0.33% to 50,182.95. The Nasdaq, which is heavy with technology firms, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80.

The day was very bumpy. At one point the Dow was down more than 1,100 points, and the Nasdaq was down 4.6%. Investors had been selling shares in companies linked to artificial intelligence, worried they may be overpriced. Prices then recovered, helped by quiet trading before the Thanksgiving holiday.

Investors also had two other worries: new tariffs, which are taxes on imports, proposed by the US, and inflation, which means rising prices. US markets are closed on Thursday for the holiday.
levels.why: What happens to US shares can affect pensions and investments here too.

levels.headline: Most US shares ended the day a little lower after a bumpy ride
levels.body:
On Wednesday 25 November, the main US share indexes ended with small moves. An index is a score that shows how a group of shares is doing. The S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7,182.78. The Nasdaq, full of technology firms, fell 0.62%. The Dow rose 0.33% to 50,182.95.

During the day things were much wilder. Early on, the Dow was down by more than 1,100 points. Many people were selling shares in artificial intelligence companies because they feared those shares had become too expensive. Later the prices came back up. It was a quiet day before the US holiday of Thanksgiving, so fewer people were trading.

Investors were also nervous about new plans for US taxes on imports, called tariffs, and about prices rising faster than expected.
levels.why: Share prices can affect the value of people's savings and pensions.

levels.headline: US shares end the day a little changed after big ups and downs
levels.body:
On Wednesday, US share prices went up and down a lot but ended almost where they began. Shares are small parts of companies that people can buy. Groups of them are tracked by scores called indexes.

The S&P 500 index fell a little, by 0.25%. The Nasdaq index, which has many tech companies, fell by 0.62%. The Dow index went up by 0.33%.

Earlier in the day the Dow was down by more than 1,100 points. That is a big drop. Many people sold shares in artificial intelligence firms because they worried the prices were too high. Later, prices bounced back. Thursday is a holiday in the US called Thanksgiving, so markets are shut.

People also worried about new US taxes on goods from other countries, and about prices going up.
levels.why: Moves in share prices can change the value of savings and pensions.

levels.headline: US share prices swing wildly but end the day close to where they began
levels.body:
Share prices in the US went up and down a lot on Wednesday, but ended close to where they started. A share is a small piece of a company. An index is a score that tracks a group of shares.

The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 big companies, ended down 0.25%. The Nasdaq index, which has many tech firms, ended down 0.62%. The Dow index went up 0.33%.

Earlier in the day the Dow was down by more than 1,100 points. People had been selling shares in artificial intelligence companies because they worried the prices were too high. Later, prices came back up. Trading was quiet because Thursday is the US holiday of Thanksgiving.

People were also worried about new taxes on imports, called tariffs, and about prices rising too fast.
levels.why: Share prices can change the value of savings and pensions.

levels.headline: US share prices went up and down but ended close to where they started
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. When many people want to buy, the price goes up. When many want to sell, it goes down. Sometimes experts add many share prices together into a score called an index.

On Wednesday, the S&P 500 score went down a little. The Nasdaq score also went down a little. The Dow score went up a little. But earlier the scores had dropped a lot. People were selling shares in computer and artificial intelligence companies. They were worried those shares cost too much.

Later in the day, the scores bounced back up. Fewer people were trading because Thursday is a big US holiday called Thanksgiving. Markets are closed that day.

People are also worried about new taxes on goods that come from other countries.
levels.why: Share prices matter because they affect people's savings and pensions.

levels.headline: Share prices bounced around but ended almost the same
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. If you own a share, you own a little bit of that company. The price of a share goes up and down every day.

On Wednesday, many share prices in America dropped a lot in the morning. Lots of people sold shares in companies that make computers and artificial intelligence. They worried those shares cost too much. Then, later in the day, the prices climbed back up.

By the end of the day, two scores that measure share prices were down a tiny bit. One was up a tiny bit. It was nearly the same as the day before.

On Thursday the shops for shares in America are closed. It is a big holiday there called Thanksgiving.
levels.why: Share prices matter because grown-ups save money in them for the future.

levels.headline: Share prices wobbled like a seesaw and ended almost level
levels.body:
Imagine a seesaw in the playground. It goes up and down, and sometimes it ends up almost level again. That is what happened to share prices in America on Wednesday.

A share is a tiny piece of a company, like owning one slice of a very big pizza. People buy and sell these slices every day. In the morning, lots of people sold slices in computer companies because they thought they cost too much. The prices dropped fast.

Later, the seesaw came back up. By the end of the day, some prices were a tiny bit lower and some were a tiny bit higher. It ended nearly where it started.

On Thursday, the share shops in America are shut for a holiday.
levels.why: Share prices can go up and down, and grown-ups keep an eye on them to look after their savings.

headline: US proposes new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the EU and India

terms.meaning: A tax on goods brought in from other countries.
A US trade law letting it respond to practices it deems unfair.
The standard tariff rates a country charges its trading partners.

levels.headline: US proposes new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the EU and India
levels.body:
The US Trade Representative has proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. They are proposed rates, not yet in force, and the USTR gave no date for them to take effect.

The tariffs rest on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, after the Supreme Court ruled in February against President Trump's earlier broad tariffs. Rates mostly range from 15% to 20%. The USTR's Jamieson Greer said they are not really additive and generally will not stack on existing duties. Proposed rates include 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia and Thailand, 20% on China and Vietnam, and 17% on India if it reaches a trade deal, up to 25% if not. The EU faces 15% on top of standard duties, possibly 20%. China could face up to 40% if talks fail.

Public comments are due by 5 January 2027 and hearings begin on 25 January.
levels.why: Tariffs raise import prices and can reshape global trade and growth.

levels.headline: US proposes fresh tariffs on 14 trading partners, with rates mostly between 15% and 20%
levels.body:
The US Trade Representative has proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. The rates are proposals only, and no start date has been given.

They are based on Section 301 of a 1974 trade law, after the Supreme Court ruled in February against the President's earlier broad tariffs. Rates mostly run from 15% to 20%. Officials say they will generally not stack on top of existing duties. China and Vietnam face 20%, Bangladesh, Cambodia and Thailand 18%, and India 17% if it agrees a trade deal, or up to 25% without one. The EU would face 15%, rising possibly to 20%. China could face up to 40% if talks fail.

The public can comment until 5 January 2027, and hearings start on 25 January.
levels.why: Higher tariffs can push up prices and disrupt trade for firms and shoppers worldwide.

levels.headline: The US proposes new import taxes on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
levels.body:
The US has proposed new tariffs, which are taxes on imported goods, on 14 trading partners. They include China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. These are only proposals and the US has not said when they might start.

The plan uses an older trade law, Section 301, after the Supreme Court ruled against the President's earlier broad tariffs in February. Most proposed rates are between 15% and 20%, and officials say they will generally not be added on top of existing duties. China and Vietnam would face 20%. The EU would face 15%, possibly rising to 20%. India would face 17% if it agrees a trade deal, and up to 25% if not. China could face up to 40% if talks fail.

People can comment until 5 January 2027, and hearings begin on 25 January.
levels.why: Tariffs can raise the price of goods and affect jobs and trade around the world.

levels.headline: The US proposes new taxes on goods from 14 trading partners
levels.body:
The United States has proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 countries and trading partners. A tariff is a tax on goods brought in from abroad. The list includes China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. These are only proposals for now, and no start date has been set.

The US is using an older trade law called Section 301. It is doing so after the Supreme Court ruled in February that the President's earlier, wider tariffs were not allowed. Most proposed rates are between 15% and 20%. China and Vietnam would face 20%, and the EU 15%, which could rise to 20%. India could face 17% if it reaches a trade deal. China could face up to 40% if talks fail.

The public can comment until 5 January 2027, and hearings begin on 25 January.
levels.why: Import taxes can make goods cost more and can change which countries trade with each other.

levels.headline: The US wants to charge new taxes on goods from 14 countries
levels.body:
The US government has said it wants to put new taxes, called tariffs, on goods coming in from 14 trading partners. These include China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. Nothing has started yet. These are plans, and no date has been set.

The US had tariffs before, but in February the Supreme Court said the President's wide ones were not allowed. So officials are using a different trade law, called Section 301, to try again. Most of the new rates would be between 15% and 20% of the goods' value. For China, the rate could go as high as 40% if talks fail.

People and firms can send their views until 5 January 2027. Hearings start on 25 January.
levels.why: Taxes on imports can make things cost more and can upset trade between countries.

levels.headline: The US plans new taxes on imports from 14 trading partners
levels.body:
The US government has proposed new taxes, called tariffs, on goods coming in from 14 trading partners, including China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. They are only plans, and no start date has been set.

Earlier this year, in February, the US Supreme Court ruled against the President's wide tariffs. So officials are now using an older trade law, called Section 301, to try again. For most countries the new taxes would be between 15% and 20% of the value of the goods. The EU would face 15%, and China 20%, which could go up to 40% if talks fail.

Tariffs are paid by firms that bring in the goods, and those firms often pass the cost on to shoppers. The public can comment until 5 January 2027. Hearings start on 25 January.
levels.why: Taxes on imports can make things cost more and upset trade between countries.

levels.headline: The US plans new taxes on things bought from 14 countries
levels.body:
The US government wants to put new taxes on goods that come from 14 other countries or groups. These taxes are called tariffs. They include China, the EU, India, Japan and South Korea. Nothing has started yet, because this is only a plan.

The US had tariffs before. In February, though, its top court said the President's wide ones were not allowed. So officials are now using a different law to try again. For most countries, the tax would be between 15% and 20% of the price of the goods. China could face up to 40% if talks go badly.

The US says people can tell the government what they think until 5 January. Meetings about it begin on 25 January.
levels.why: Taxes on imports can make things in shops cost more.

levels.headline: The US wants to charge extra on goods from 14 countries
levels.body:
The US wants to put an extra tax on goods that come from 14 countries and groups of countries. This kind of tax is called a tariff. Think of it as a fee that shops must pay to bring things in from abroad. Those shops then often make the price for buyers higher.

The countries include China, India, Japan and the EU. This is only a plan for now. The US has not said when it would start.

Last time, in February, the top court in the US said the President's wide tax plan was not allowed. So now officials are trying a different law. Most of the new taxes would be between 15 and 20 out of every 100 of the goods' price.

The US will listen to people's views until 5 January.
levels.why: Extra taxes on goods can make things cost more and can cause arguments between countries.

levels.headline: The US plans a new fee on goods from 14 countries
levels.body:
A tariff is a kind of fee. When a shop brings toys or clothes into a country from abroad, the government can make the shop pay a fee. That often makes the things cost more for people who buy them.

The US government wants to add new fees on goods from 14 places. They include China, India, Japan and the countries of the EU. It is only a plan so far. Nothing will change right away.

The US tried to do this before. Then its top court, a bit like a very important judge, said that plan was not allowed. So now the government is trying a new way.

The fee would be about 15 to 20 out of every 100 pounds' worth of goods, for most places. The government says it will listen to people's thoughts first.
levels.why: It matters because fees on imports can make things in the shops cost more.

levels.headline: The US plans extra fees on things from other countries
levels.body:
Imagine a school tuck shop that buys sweets from a big warehouse far away. Now imagine someone says, "Each time you bring in sweets, you must pay a fee." The tuck shop would probably put up its prices to cover the fee.

That is a bit like a tariff. The US wants to add new fees on goods from 14 places, like China, India, Japan and Europe. It is only a plan, not a rule yet. The people in charge will listen to what others think first.

The US tried something like this before. But its top court, which is like the head referee, said the old plan was not allowed. So now the US is trying a new way to make the same sort of plan.

If it happens, some things in shops might cost a bit more.
levels.why: If it happens, some things in shops could cost a bit more, so people are watching closely.

headline: UK borrowing was £17.0 billion in October as debt interest jumped a third and debt passed £3.05 trillion

terms.meaning: The gap when government spends more than it raises in a period.
The cost of paying interest on money the government has borrowed.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster of the public finances.

levels.headline: UK borrowing was £17.0 billion in October as debt interest jumped a third and debt passed £3.05 trillion
levels.body:
UK public sector net borrowing was £17.0 billion in October, £0.8 billion (5.2%) more than a year earlier, the Office for National Statistics said on 20 November. It was the third-highest October since monthly records began in 1993, behind 2024 and 2020.

Central government debt interest rose £2.8 billion (33.4%) from a year earlier to £11.2 billion. Borrowing from April to October totalled £111.3 billion, which is £7.3 billion (6.1%) less than in the same period of 2025 but £3.3 billion above the Office for Budget Responsibility's March forecast.

Public sector net debt was provisionally estimated at £3,058.3 billion at the end of October. Trading Economics noted that October borrowing came in below the £18.0 billion analysts expected. The ONS says the figures are provisional and may be revised. The next release is due on 22 December.
levels.why: Borrowing and debt interest limit what the government can spend or cut taxes on.

levels.headline: UK borrowing hits £17.0 billion in October, with debt interest up by a third
levels.body:
The UK government borrowed £17.0 billion in October, £0.8 billion more than a year earlier, according to the ONS in figures published on 20 November. It was the third-highest October figure since monthly records began in 1993.

The cost of paying interest on government debt rose by £2.8 billion, or 33.4%, to £11.2 billion. Borrowing for the first seven months of the financial year, from April to October, was £111.3 billion. That is £7.3 billion less than a year earlier, but £3.3 billion above what the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, predicted in March.

Total public sector net debt was provisionally put at £3,058.3 billion. October borrowing was below the £18.0 billion analysts expected. The figures may be revised, and the next release is on 22 December.
levels.why: It shows how tight the public finances are, which shapes tax and spending choices.

levels.headline: UK government borrowing was £17 billion in October, and interest costs are rising fast
levels.body:
The UK government borrowed £17.0 billion in October, which is £0.8 billion more than the same month last year. The Office for National Statistics published the figures on 20 November. It was the third-highest October since records began in 1993.

The bill for interest on the government's debt jumped by a third, up £2.8 billion to £11.2 billion. Over the financial year so far, from April to October, borrowing was £111.3 billion. That is less than a year ago, but £3.3 billion more than the government's official forecaster expected in March.

The country's total debt is now about £3.06 trillion. Analysts had expected October borrowing to be £18.0 billion, so it was a little better than feared. The figures are provisional and could change.
levels.why: Rising interest costs leave less money for public services and tax cuts.

levels.headline: The UK borrowed £17 billion in October, and the cost of its debt keeps growing
levels.body:
The UK government borrowed £17.0 billion in October, according to official figures out on 20 November. Borrowing means spending more than it collects in taxes. This was £0.8 billion more than a year before, and the third-highest for any October since records began in 1993.

One big reason is interest. The government pays interest on the money it has already borrowed, like a credit card bill. That cost rose by a third, up £2.8 billion to £11.2 billion in a month.

Since April, borrowing has totalled £111.3 billion. That is less than last year, but £3.3 billion above what the official forecaster expected in March. The country's total debt is about £3.06 trillion. The figures may be revised later.
levels.why: Paying more interest leaves less money for schools, hospitals and tax cuts.

levels.headline: The UK borrowed £17 billion in October, and paying interest on its debts costs more and more
levels.body:
The UK government borrowed £17 billion in October. That means it spent £17 billion more than it received in taxes and other income that month. The figure comes from the Office for National Statistics, which published it on 20 November. Only two earlier Octobers had higher borrowing since records began in 1993.

Part of the reason is interest. When the government borrows, it must pay interest, a bit like on a loan. That bill was £11.2 billion in October, a third more than a year ago.

Since April, total borrowing has been £111.3 billion. That is lower than last year, but higher than the government's official forecasters expected. Total government debt is now about £3.06 trillion, which is £3,058 billion.
levels.why: The more the government pays in interest, the less it has for services and tax cuts.

levels.headline: The UK government borrowed £17 billion in October, and the interest bill is growing
levels.body:
In October, the UK government spent £17 billion more than it took in. When this happens, it has to borrow money to cover the gap. The numbers came out on 20 November.

The government already owes a lot, about £3 trillion in total. Like anyone who borrows, it has to pay interest on that. In October the interest bill was £11.2 billion. A year ago it was much lower, and it has gone up by a third.

Since April, the government has borrowed £111.3 billion. That is less than at this point last year. But it is a bit more than official forecasters thought it would be.

When more money goes on interest, there is less left for things like schools and hospitals.
levels.why: Money spent on interest cannot be spent on things like schools, hospitals or tax cuts.

levels.headline: The UK government spent £17 billion more than it earned in October
levels.body:
Governments get money from taxes. They spend it on things like schools, hospitals and roads. Some months they spend more than they get. To cover the gap, they borrow. In October the UK government borrowed £17 billion.

The government already owes about £3 trillion. That is a very big number. Just as you pay back more when you borrow from a bank, the government must pay extra, called interest. In October the interest was £11.2 billion. That is a third more than a year ago.

Since April, the government has borrowed £111.3 billion. That is a bit less than last year. It is more than experts guessed in March, though.

If a lot of money goes on interest, there is less left for other things.
levels.why: Money spent paying interest cannot go on things like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The government borrowed £17 billion in October and has to pay extra to borrow
levels.body:
Sometimes a family spends more money than it earns in a month. To fill the gap, they might borrow. The UK government does the same. Last month, it borrowed £17 billion.

The government has borrowed a lot over the years. It owes about £3 trillion. When you borrow, you have to pay a bit extra, called interest. Last month the government paid £11.2 billion in interest. That is a third more than a year ago.

People who count these things said the numbers on 20 November. They also said the government has borrowed £111 billion since April. That is a little less than last year.

When more money goes on interest, there is less left for fun and useful things like new hospitals.
levels.why: The more the government pays for borrowing, the less there is for things that help people.

levels.headline: The country borrowed a very big pile of money again last month
levels.body:
Imagine your family spends more than it earns and so borrows from a bank. The UK does that too, but with much bigger numbers. In October, the UK government borrowed £17 billion. That is 17 thousand million pounds.

When you borrow, you must give back the money and a little extra, called interest. Think of it like paying a small fee to borrow someone's toys. The UK has borrowed so much over the years that the extra fee is now £11.2 billion in a month. That is a third more than last year.

The more money that goes on the extra fee, the less is left for good things like schools, parks and hospitals.
levels.why: If less money goes on borrowing costs, more could go on things like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The UK borrowed lots of money, like a very big pocket-money loan
levels.body:
Imagine you spend more pocket money than you get. To keep going, you borrow some from your big sister. The UK government did something like this last month. It borrowed £17 billion. That is a huge amount.

When you borrow from your sister, she might ask for a little extra back as a thank-you. This is called interest. The government has borrowed so much that the extra it has to pay is now £11.2 billion in one month. That is a third more than a year ago.

The more the government pays in extras, the less it has left for things like schools, hospitals and parks.

Grown-ups keep a careful eye on this, so that the loan does not get too big.
levels.why: Grown-ups watch borrowing so there is enough money left for schools and hospitals.

headline: Farage accuses Burnham of betraying Brexit as the prime minister says an EU rejoin referendum is 'possible' in a future manifesto

levels.headline: Farage accuses Burnham of betraying Brexit as the prime minister says an EU rejoin referendum is 'possible' in a future manifesto
levels.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying Brexit voters as the EU-UK summit began in Brussels on 20 November. Farage said the deal pulls Britain back into parts of the single market, particularly food and farming, breaking Labour's promise not to rejoin it. He argued Britain would have to accept EU rules without a vote on them.

Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" that a referendum on rejoining the EU could feature in a future election manifesto. He has also said a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now", and has floated options from a customs union to the single market, or going "all the way". Farage said that if Burnham fought an election on rejoining, he would have to hold a referendum.

One YouGov survey found 56% of British voters would support rejoining. Coverage shows no formal manifesto commitment either way.
levels.why: The row shows how far Britain's relationship with the EU is again a central political fight.

levels.headline: Farage says Burnham has betrayed Brexit voters, as the PM keeps the door open to an EU referendum
levels.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying Brexit voters. He made the claim as the EU-UK summit got under way in Brussels on 20 November. He said the deal takes Britain back into parts of the single market, mainly food and farming, which he argued breaks a Labour promise. He said Britain would follow EU rules without a say.

Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" a referendum on rejoining the EU could be in a future election manifesto. He has also said such a vote "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now". He has mentioned options from a customs union to the single market, or going "all the way".

One YouGov poll found 56% of voters would back rejoining. No formal manifesto promise has been made.
levels.why: It shows the next election could be shaped by arguments over Brexit.

levels.headline: Farage accuses Burnham of betraying Brexit as the PM does not rule out an EU vote
levels.body:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, has accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying people who voted for Brexit. He spoke on 20 November, as UK and EU leaders met in Brussels. Farage said the new deals bring Britain back into parts of the single market, the EU's shared trading area, especially for food and farming. He said that breaks a Labour promise and that Britain would have to follow EU rules with no vote on them.

Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" that a vote on rejoining the EU could be in a future manifesto, which is a party's list of election promises. But he has also said a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

One YouGov poll found 56% of voters would support rejoining.
levels.why: The argument could shape how people vote in the next election.

levels.headline: Farage says the PM has betrayed Brexit, and Burnham will not rule out a vote on rejoining the EU
levels.body:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, says Prime Minister Andy Burnham has betrayed people who voted for Brexit. He said this on 20 November, as UK and EU leaders met in Brussels. Farage argues that the new deals take Britain back into parts of the single market, which is the EU's shared trading area. He says the UK would have to follow EU rules without any say.

Mr Burnham told the BBC that it was "possible" a vote on rejoining the EU could be in a future manifesto. A manifesto is a party's list of promises before an election. But he also said a referendum, a vote for everyone, "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

One YouGov poll found 56% of voters would back rejoining. No promise has been made.
levels.why: It shows Brexit is still one of the biggest arguments in British politics.

levels.headline: Nigel Farage says the PM has let down Brexit voters, but Burnham says nothing is decided
levels.body:
Nigel Farage, who leads the party Reform UK, says the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has let down people who voted for Brexit. He said so on 20 November, when UK and EU leaders met in Brussels. Mr Farage says the new deals pull Britain back towards the EU's shared market for goods. He says Britain would have to follow EU rules without any say in making them.

Mr Burnham told the BBC that it was possible a vote on rejoining the EU could be one of his party's promises at a future election. But he also said a vote "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

One poll, by YouGov, found that 56% of people would support rejoining. Nothing has been promised yet.
levels.why: The argument could shape how people vote at the next election.

levels.headline: Farage says Burnham has let down Brexit voters, and the PM says a rejoin vote is possible one day
levels.body:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, says Prime Minister Andy Burnham has let down the people who voted for Brexit. He said so on 20 November, when UK and EU leaders met in Brussels. He argues that the new deals pull Britain back towards the EU's shared market, so the UK would have to follow EU rules without a say in them.

Mr Burnham told the BBC that it was possible a vote on rejoining the EU could be in his party's promises at a future election. He also said that a vote would not be right at the moment. He has talked about different steps Britain could take, such as a customs union, which is a deal to share the same import taxes.

One poll found 56% of people would support rejoining. Nothing has been promised.
levels.why: It shows Brexit is still a big argument in British politics.

levels.headline: Nigel Farage says the PM has let down people who wanted Brexit
levels.body:
The UK left the EU in 2020. Many people voted for that, and they are called Brexit voters. On 20 November, a politician called Nigel Farage said that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has let them down.

Mr Farage says the new deals bring Britain closer to the EU again. He says Britain might have to follow EU rules without being able to help make them. He does not like this.

Mr Burnham told the BBC that one day his party might promise a vote on rejoining the EU. But he also said that now is not the right time. Nothing has been decided.

One poll asked people about rejoining. More than half of them, 56 out of every 100, said they would support it.
levels.why: It shows many people still disagree about how close Britain should be to Europe.

levels.headline: A leader says the prime minister has let down people who wanted to leave the EU
levels.body:
A few years ago, the UK left the EU. The EU is a group of countries in Europe. Lots of people voted to leave. On 20 November, a politician called Nigel Farage said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has let those people down.

Mr Farage says the new deals bring Britain closer to the EU again. He thinks that is wrong. He says Britain would have to follow rules without helping to make them.

Mr Burnham was asked if the UK might ever vote on joining the EU again. He said that is possible one day. But he said that now is not the right time.

One poll found that more than half of people, 56 out of 100, would like to rejoin.
levels.why: It shows people still disagree about how close Britain should be to Europe.

levels.headline: People disagree about how close the UK should be to Europe
levels.body:
The UK used to be in a group of countries called the EU. A few years ago, it left. Some people were very happy about that. Others were sad.

Now the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has made some new deals with the EU. A politician called Nigel Farage says that is wrong. He thinks the prime minister is letting down the people who wanted to leave.

The prime minister says that one day his party might ask everyone to vote about joining again. But he says it is not the right time now. No vote has been planned.

In one poll, more than half the people asked said they would like to rejoin. But people have many different views.
levels.why: It matters because people have strong and different views about this.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are still arguing about whether to be friends with Europe
levels.body:
Imagine a group of friends. A few years ago, one friend, the UK, decided to leave the group. Some people thought that was a good idea. Others did not.

Now the leader of the UK, Andy Burnham, wants to work together with the group a bit more. A man called Nigel Farage is cross. He thinks the leader is letting down the people who wanted to leave.

The leader says he might ask everyone to vote on joining again one day. But he says now is not the right time.

When people disagree, like in the playground, they sometimes need to talk it through. Grown-ups will keep talking about this one for a long time.
levels.why: It matters because people have different views, and grown-ups must find a way to agree.

headline: UK tariff suspensions on groceries start today, part of Healey's Budget that cut energy bills and taxed banks

An extra tax charged on banks' profits.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster of the public finances.

levels.headline: UK tariff suspensions on groceries start today, part of Healey's Budget that cut energy bills and taxed banks
levels.body:
Tariff suspensions on selected food products and kerosene heating oil take effect today, 26 November, under the Budget announced on 28 October by the chancellor, John Healey. The government says tariffs on more than 100 grocery products are being removed.

The Budget also removes standing charges from household gas heating bills, extends an electricity tax break to July 2027, and sends £100 payments to households in the four lowest council tax bands. To help pay, the bank surcharge was raised to 6%, and banks, gambling businesses and vape shops face higher taxes. The minimum wage rises by 3.9%.

The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year, 1% in 2027 and 1.6% in 2028, and forecasts £15 billion of fiscal headroom by 2029/30. National debt has passed £3 trillion. The Budget also needs a plan to lift defence spending to 3% of GDP by the end of the decade.
levels.why: The measures change what households pay for food and energy and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: Cuts to some grocery import taxes start today as part of the autumn Budget
levels.body:
Suspensions of tariffs on selected food products and kerosene heating oil begin today, 26 November. They were announced in the Budget delivered by the chancellor, John Healey, on 28 October. The government says duties on more than 100 grocery products are being removed.

The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts growth of 1.2% this year, 1% next year and 1.6% in 2028, with £15 billion of headroom by 2029/30. National debt has risen above £3 trillion.
levels.why: It affects household bills and shows how the government balances help for families with its finances.

levels.headline: Import taxes on more than 100 grocery items are suspended from today under the Budget
levels.body:
From today, 26 November, tariffs on some food products and on kerosene heating oil are suspended. This comes from the Budget announced on 28 October by the chancellor, John Healey. The government says tariffs on more than 100 grocery products are being removed.

The Budget also takes standing charges off household gas heating bills, extends a tax break on electricity until July 2027, and gives £100 to households in the four lowest council tax bands. To pay for this, the tax on bank profits, the bank surcharge, goes up to 6%. Banks, gambling firms and vape shops also face higher taxes. The minimum wage rises by 3.9%.

The official forecaster expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year. Government debt has passed £3 trillion.
levels.why: These changes should lower some household costs, but the government has to pay for them.

levels.headline: Taxes on over 100 food items are cut from today as the Budget measures begin
levels.body:
From today, 26 November, some import taxes on food are suspended. These are called tariffs. They also apply to kerosene, a fuel used for heating. The change comes from the Budget on 28 October, delivered by the chancellor, John Healey. In total, over 100 grocery products are affected.

The Budget has other help with bills. Standing charges, the fixed daily fee on gas heating, are removed. A tax break on electricity is extended until July 2027. Households in the four lowest council tax bands get £100. To pay for this, banks will pay a higher extra tax on profits, now 6%. Gambling firms and vape shops will pay more tax too. The minimum wage goes up 3.9%.

Official forecasters expect the economy to grow 1.2% this year.
levels.why: Lower tariffs and bill support aim to ease the pressure on household budgets.

levels.headline: Some food and heating taxes are cut from today as the Budget starts to bite
levels.body:
From today, 26 November, some taxes on imported food are cut. These taxes are called tariffs. More than 100 grocery items are affected. A tax on kerosene, used for heating, is also cut. These changes come from the Budget on 28 October. The chancellor, John Healey, announced it.

The Budget also aims to cut bills. The fixed daily fee on gas heating, called a standing charge, is removed. A tax break on electricity lasts until July 2027. Some households get £100 as well.

To pay for this, banks will pay more tax on their profits. Gambling firms and vape shops will pay more too. The minimum wage rises by 3.9%. The government also owes more than £3 trillion, so it has to be careful with money.
levels.why: These changes could lower some bills, but the government must find the money to pay for them.

levels.headline: Some food and heating costs fall from today as new Budget plans begin
levels.body:
Some food in the shops could get cheaper. From today, 26 November, the government has paused some taxes on food from abroad. These taxes are called tariffs. They cover more than 100 grocery items. Heating oil is included too.

This comes from the Budget. A Budget is the government's plan for how it will collect and spend money. This one was announced on 28 October by the chancellor, John Healey. He is in charge of the government's money.

The Budget also takes off a fixed fee on gas heating bills. It gives £100 to some households. And it raises the minimum wage by 3.9%.

To pay for it, banks and some other firms will pay more tax. The government still owes more than £3 trillion.
levels.why: These plans aim to help families with the cost of living.

levels.headline: Some food costs less from today because of new government plans
levels.body:
Every year the government makes a plan for how it will get and spend money. This plan is called the Budget. This year's was announced on 28 October by John Healey, the person in charge of the government's money.

From today, 26 November, some of the taxes on food coming from other countries are paused. Over 100 grocery items are covered. That could make some food cost a little less.

The plan also takes away a fixed fee on gas heating bills. Some families get £100. The lowest pay a worker can get, called the minimum wage, goes up too.

To pay for this, banks and some other firms will pay more tax. The government is also careful because it already owes a huge amount of money.
levels.why: The plans aim to help families with the cost of food and heating.

levels.headline: Some food will cost a bit less from today
levels.body:
Every year the government makes a plan for money. It says how much tax to collect and what to spend it on. The plan is called the Budget. This year's was shared on 28 October.

From today, some taxes on food from other countries are paused. More than 100 kinds of food in shops are affected. That could make some of them cost less. Heating oil is included too.

The plan also takes away a fixed fee on gas heating. Some families get £100. Workers on the lowest pay will get a pay rise.

To pay for it, banks and a few other businesses will pay more tax. The government is also careful. It already owes a very large amount of money.
levels.why: The plan is meant to help families pay for food and heating.

levels.headline: The government is making some food and heating cheaper
levels.body:
Do you know that a country has a pot of money, called its budget? It comes from taxes that people and companies pay. The government decides how to spend it. This year, it said it will spend some to help families.

From today, some taxes on food from other countries are stopped for a while. This could make some food in the shops cost less. Fixed fees on gas heating are taken away too. Some families get £100.

To fill the pot again, banks and some other firms will pay more tax.

The aim is to make life a little easier for families when things cost a lot. Grown-ups will see how well it works.
levels.why: It is meant to make life a bit easier for families when things cost a lot.

levels.headline: The government is giving families a little help with bills
levels.body:
Think of the country's money like the class tuck shop fund. Everyone puts a little in, and a teacher decides how to use it. The government does the same with taxes. It has just said how it will use some of the money this year.

From today, some food from other countries gets a tax break, so it may cost less in shops. Heating bills lose a fixed fee. Some families get £100 as a helping hand.

But the money has to come from somewhere. So banks and a few other firms will pay a bit more into the fund. It is like asking the people with the biggest piggy banks to put in a little extra.

Grown-ups will watch to see if it helps.
levels.why: It is meant to help families when things cost a lot.

headline: Representation of the People Bill, which would give 16-year-olds the vote in all UK elections, reaches the Lords committee stage

The official list of people entitled to vote.

levels.headline: Representation of the People Bill, which would give 16-year-olds the vote in all UK elections, reaches the Lords committee stage
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has entered Lords Committee Stage, where peers examine its measures in detail. It was introduced to Parliament on 12 February 2026, and the government wants it in force in time for the next general election.

Its central change is to extend the voting age to 16 for all UK elections, bringing them in line with Scotland and Wales. The registration age would be lowered to 14, so people can be registered if an election falls on or shortly after their 16th birthday. Under-16s would not appear on any public version of the electoral register and could not opt in to the open register. Some 16- and 17-year-olds already registered for devolved elections in Scotland and Wales could be added to the UK Parliament register without a fresh application.

The bill also contains tougher rules on political donations and foreign interference. No Lords votes have been reported yet.
levels.why: It would change who can vote at general elections and add up to two years of young voters.

levels.headline: Bill giving 16-year-olds the vote in every UK election moves to detailed scrutiny in the Lords
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has reached Lords Committee Stage, when peers go through it clause by clause. It was introduced on 12 February 2026, and the government wants the law in place before the next general election.

The main change is a voting age of 16 for all UK elections, matching Scotland and Wales. People could register from age 14, so that someone who turns 16 around polling day is ready to vote. Under-16s would be hidden from the public register and could not join the open register. Some 16- and 17-year-olds already registered for devolved elections would be added to the UK Parliament register automatically.

The bill also tightens rules on political donations and foreign interference. No votes in the Lords have yet been reported.
levels.why: It could bring younger people into general elections for the first time.

levels.headline: The bill to give 16-year-olds the vote at general elections is now being examined by peers
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16-year-olds vote in every UK election has reached the House of Lords committee stage. This is when peers study the bill in detail. The Representation of the People Bill was introduced on 12 February. The government wants it to be law before the next general election.

At the moment, 16-year-olds can vote in Scotland and Wales for some elections, but not for the UK Parliament. The bill would change that. People could also sign up to the register from age 14. Details of under-16s would not appear on the public register. Some 16- and 17-year-olds already registered in Scotland or Wales would be added to the UK register without applying again.

The bill also brings in tougher rules on political donations and foreign interference.
levels.why: It could change who takes part in the next general election.

levels.headline: Peers begin detailed checks on the bill to lower the voting age to 16
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16-year-olds vote in all UK elections has reached the House of Lords committee stage. This is when peers look at each part of a bill in detail. The government introduced the Representation of the People Bill on 12 February. It wants the law to be ready before the next general election.

At the moment, 16-year-olds can vote in some elections in Scotland and Wales. They cannot vote in UK general elections. The bill would change that. It would also let young people sign up to the electoral register, the official list of voters, at 14. Under-16s would not be on the public version of the list.

The bill also includes tougher rules on political donations and on interference from other countries.
levels.why: It could mean millions of young people get a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A law to let 16-year-olds vote is being checked by the House of Lords
levels.body:
A new bill would let 16-year-olds vote in all UK elections. It is now being checked in detail by the House of Lords. That is the part of Parliament where peers, who are not elected, look closely at new laws and suggest changes. The bill is called the Representation of the People Bill. The government wants it to be law before the next general election.

At the moment, 16-year-olds can vote in some elections in Scotland and Wales, but not in general elections. The bill would change that for the whole UK. Young people could also add their names to the voting list from age 14, so they are ready when they turn 16.

The bill also has tougher rules on money given to political parties.
levels.why: It could give young people a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: Plan to let 16-year-olds vote in every UK election is being checked by peers
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16-year-olds vote in all UK elections is being checked in detail by the House of Lords. It is called the Representation of the People Bill, and the government introduced it on 12 February. It wants the law in place before the next general election.

Today, 16-year-olds can vote in some elections in Scotland and Wales, but not in general elections. The bill would change that, so the voting age is the same across the UK. Young people could also add their names to the electoral register, the official list of voters, from the age of 14. That would make sure that anyone turning 16 around polling day is ready to vote. Under-16s would not be on the public list.

The bill also tightens the rules on political donations and on interference from other countries.
levels.why: It could give younger people a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A bill that would let 16-year-olds vote is now being studied in the House of Lords
levels.body:
Right now you must be 18 to vote in a general election. A new law, the Representation of the People Bill, would lower that to 16 for all elections in the UK. In Scotland and Wales, 16-year-olds can already vote in some elections.

Before a bill becomes law, both parts of Parliament have to agree to it. It is now in the House of Lords. There, people called peers go through it carefully and may suggest changes. The government hopes it will become law before the next general election.

The bill also lets young people put their names on the voting list from the age of 14. That way they are ready when they turn 16. It has tougher rules on party donations too.
levels.why: It would give younger people a say in decisions that affect them.

levels.headline: A new law might let 16-year-olds vote in elections
levels.body:
Elections are when people vote for who they want to run the country. At the moment you have to be 18 to vote in a general election. A new law, called a bill, would change that to 16.

A bill has to be checked before it becomes a law. Right now, a group called the House of Lords is going through it slowly. They check each part to see if it makes sense. They can ask for changes.

In Scotland and Wales, 16-year-olds can already vote in some elections. The new law would let them vote in all of them across the UK.

The bill would also let you put your name on the voting list at 14. That way you are ready when you turn 16.
levels.why: It would mean younger people get a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A new rule could mean you can vote when you are 16
levels.body:
In this country, grown-ups vote to choose who runs it. This is called an election. Now you must be 18 to vote in the biggest ones. People in government want to change that to 16.

Before a new rule is made, many people have to check it. Some of them sit in a big old room called the House of Lords. They read the rule slowly and ask questions. They are doing that now.

In Scotland and Wales, 16-year-olds can already vote in some elections. The new rule would be for the whole country.

Young people would also be able to put their name on the voting list when they turn 14. That way they are ready to vote at 16.
levels.why: It could mean young people can help choose who runs the country.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are checking a rule that might let teenagers vote
levels.body:
To vote, you must be old enough. At the moment, that means 18 for the biggest votes in this country. Some people want to change it to 16, so teenagers can have a say too.

Before a new rule begins, a group of grown-ups has to check it. They are a bit like teachers marking homework. They read it carefully and say if something needs fixing. Right now, a group called the House of Lords is checking this one.

If it becomes a rule, it would work like this. When you turn 16, you could help choose who runs the country. You would put your name on a list a little earlier, so you are ready.

It is not decided yet.
levels.why: It could let teenagers have a say in who runs the country.

headline: Brent crude jumps 3.5% to settle at $94.61 after Houthis claim attack on Saudi refinery

levels.headline: Brent crude jumps 3.5% to settle at $94.61 after Houthis claim attack on Saudi refinery
levels.body:
Brent crude futures rose 3.5% to settle at $94.61 a barrel on 25 November, according to CNBC, after the Yemeni Houthi movement said it had attacked a Saudi oil refinery. US benchmark WTI closed at $83.68. Trading Economics showed Brent about 2.9% higher on the day, and around $95.24 on 26 November.

Prices had been lower earlier in the session. Brent was down 43 cents, or 0.5%, at $90.97 by 0137 GMT, as traders weighed a projected supply surplus. The International Energy Agency expects a global surplus in the fourth quarter as output recovers faster than demand.

headline: Houthi attacks on Saudi sites injure 11 as Iran reports tankers hit mines in Hormuz and Trump threatens to strike bridges and power plants

levels.headline: Houthi attacks on Saudi sites injure 11 as Iran reports tankers hit mines in Hormuz and Trump threatens to strike bridges and power plants
levels.body:
The Yemeni Houthi movement has claimed attacks on Saudi energy sites, and a Houthi attack on the Riyadh tower of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, PIF, injured 11 people, CNBC reported. The Houthis said they targeted the Rabigh refinery on Sunday and later the Ras Tanura refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest and a major export terminal. Damage has not been confirmed, and the claims are not independently verified.

In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers hit naval mines and were burning. A UOB analyst said Iranian attacks on tankers were running at about one incident a day in November.

President Trump said that each time Iran shoots at a ship in Hormuz, the US would destroy one bridge or power plant. Iran said it would retaliate against US-linked infrastructure and energy assets in the region. Reports differ on some dates.
levels.why: Attacks on Gulf oil routes threaten global energy supplies and risk a wider war.

headline: US inflation by the Fed's preferred gauge rises to 3.8% in October, and traders see a December rate hike as fully priced

terms.meaning: Personal consumption expenditures, the price measure the US Federal Reserve prefers.

levels.headline: US inflation by the Fed's preferred gauge rises to 3.8% in October, and traders see a December rate hike as fully priced
levels.body:
The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.7% in September, CNBC reported on 25 November. Headline PCE rose 0.3% on the month. Core PCE, which strips out food and energy, was 3.3%, nearly double the Federal Reserve's 2% target.

Both readings matched forecasts, though core came in slightly above the consensus. Stock futures fell after the release. Gold dropped to its lowest level in more than a year as traders bet on higher rates. Traders now see a rate rise in December as fully priced in.

The figures arrived as markets were already unsettled by a sell-off in artificial intelligence shares and by new US tariff proposals, and as doubts grew over whether heavy AI spending can produce enough returns.
levels.why: Persistent US inflation shapes interest rates, share prices and borrowing costs worldwide.

levels.headline: The Fed's favourite inflation measure climbs to 3.8% as markets expect another interest rate rise
levels.body:
A key US inflation measure rose to 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from 3.7% in September. It is the personal consumption expenditures, or PCE, price index, the gauge the Federal Reserve prefers. Prices rose 0.3% on the month. Core PCE, which leaves out food and energy, was 3.3%, well above the Fed's 2% target.

Both figures matched expectations, though core was slightly higher than forecast. After the release, stock futures fell and gold dropped to its lowest in over a year. Traders now think a rate rise in December is fully priced in.

The data came as markets were also worried by falling AI shares and by new US tariff plans.
levels.why: It shows inflation is still high, which keeps interest rates up around the world.

levels.headline: US inflation rises to 3.8% on the Fed's preferred measure, keeping a December rate rise in view
levels.body:
A measure of US inflation that the Federal Reserve likes to watch rose to 3.8% in October, compared with a year before. In September it was 3.7%. The measure is called PCE, and it follows what people spend. Prices rose 0.3% over the month. When food and energy are left out, the figure, called core inflation, was 3.3%. The Fed aims for 2%.

The numbers were about what experts expected, though the core figure was a little higher. After they were published, share futures fell and the price of gold dropped to its lowest in more than a year. Traders now think the Fed will raise interest rates in December.

Investors were already nervous about AI shares and new US tariff plans.
levels.why: Higher inflation can mean higher interest rates and more costly borrowing.

levels.headline: US inflation edges up to 3.8%, so another interest rate rise looks likely

A key US measure of inflation, which means how fast prices are rising, went up to 3.8% in October compared with a year earlier. In September it was 3.7%. The measure is called PCE, and it is the one the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, likes best. Prices went up 0.3% in a single month. Leaving out food and energy, which can jump around, the rate was 3.3%. The Fed wants it to be 2%.

The numbers were about what people expected. Even so, share futures fell afterwards, and the price of gold dropped to its lowest in over a year. Investors now think the Fed will raise interest rates in December. Interest rates are the cost of borrowing money.
levels.why: Higher inflation can lead to higher interest rates and costlier borrowing.

levels.headline: Prices in the US are still rising faster than the central bank wants
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices rise. In the US, a measure of it went up to 3.8% in October, compared with a year earlier. In September it was 3.7%. The US central bank, called the Federal Reserve, has a goal of 2%, so this is much higher. Prices rose 0.3% in just one month. Leaving out food and energy, which can jump about, the rate was 3.3%.

Experts were not surprised. But share prices fell a little after the news, and gold got cheaper. People now think the Fed will raise interest rates in December. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money, such as for a home. A higher rate makes borrowing cost more.
levels.why: Higher inflation can mean higher interest rates and more costly borrowing.

levels.headline: US inflation rises to 3.8%, and the central bank may raise interest rates again
levels.body:
Prices in the US are going up faster than the country's central bank, the Federal Reserve, would like. A measure of inflation that the Fed prefers rose to 3.8% in October compared with a year earlier, up from 3.7% in September. The Fed's goal is 2%. Prices rose 0.3% in the month alone. Without food and energy, which can jump around, the figure was 3.3%.

The numbers were about what experts expected. Even so, share futures fell and gold dropped to its lowest price in over a year. Traders now think the Fed will raise interest rates in December.

Interest rates are the cost of borrowing money. When they go up, loans and mortgages become more expensive. The Fed does this to slow down rising prices, because people tend to spend less when borrowing costs more.
levels.why: Higher inflation can mean higher interest rates and more costly borrowing.

levels.headline: US prices are rising faster than the central bank wants, so interest rates may go up again
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up over time. In the US, it was 3.8% in October compared with a year earlier. That is the rate that the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, likes to watch. Its goal is 2%, so inflation is much higher than it wants. Prices rose 0.3% in the month alone.

Many people had expected this number, but it still worried investors. Share prices fell a little, and gold went down in price.

Now many people think the Fed will raise interest rates in December. Interest rates are the cost of borrowing money. When they go up, loans and mortgages cost more. The Fed does this to slow down rising prices, because it makes people spend a bit less.
levels.why: It matters because higher interest rates make borrowing cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in America are going up fast, so borrowing might cost more
levels.body:
When prices go up over time, we call it inflation. In America, prices were 3.8% higher in October than a year before. The people who run America's central bank want it to be 2%. So prices are going up much faster than they would like.

When this happens, the central bank can raise interest rates. An interest rate is the extra money you pay when you borrow money. If the rate goes up, you pay more extra. That makes people spend less, and so prices stop rising so fast.

Many people now think the central bank will raise rates in December.

Share prices fell a little on the news. Gold, a shiny metal that people buy and keep, also got cheaper.
levels.why: It matters because higher interest rates make borrowing cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in America keep going up, and the bank may make loans cost more
levels.body:
Think about a packet of sweets. A year ago it cost 100 pence. Now in America a packet like that costs 3.8 pence more. We call this rising price inflation. The people in charge of America's money, in the central bank, would like it to rise by only 2 pence.

When prices rise too fast, the bank can make borrowing cost more. The extra money you pay for a loan is called interest. If the bank puts up the rate of interest, people borrow less and spend less, and prices stop rising so quickly.

Many people think the bank will do this in December.

Some shares in companies got cheaper on the news.
levels.why: It matters because higher interest rates make loans cost more.

levels.headline: Prices keep creeping up, like sweets that get more expensive
levels.body:
Do you remember when your favourite sweets cost less? Over time, many things in shops cost a little more. This is called inflation.

In America, prices have gone up quite a lot over the past year. The people who look after America's money, in a place called the central bank, do not like it. They want prices to go up only slowly.

To slow things down, they can make it cost more to borrow money. The extra you pay when you borrow is called interest. When it gets bigger, people borrow less and spend less. Then prices stop going up so fast.

Many people think the bank will do this soon, maybe in December.
levels.why: It matters because it can make things cost more for families.

headline: EU proposes 22nd sanctions package targeting Russian banks, soldiers who fought in Ukraine and athletes

terms.meaning: Penalties on a country, such as limits on trade or finance.
