levels.headline: EU proposes 22nd sanctions package targeting Russian banks, soldiers who fought in Ukraine and athletes
levels.body:
The European Commission proposed its 22nd sanctions package against Russia on Monday 23 November. It would remove an additional 60 Russian banks from the SWIFT international payments system and crack down on crypto platforms.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also revived a proposed entry ban on Russian soldiers who have fought in Ukraine. An earlier attempt in July stalled after France and Italy raised concerns about administrative and legal burdens. The package would also bar Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag from sports events inside the bloc. Von der Leyen said sports events cannot be "a forum for propaganda activities".

Adoption needs the agreement of all member states, and Brussels hopes for a deal in December before the holiday break. Ukraine's sanctions envoy welcomed the plan but urged more ambition, including measures on Rosatom and alumina sales. Alumina was absent from the proposal. No final approval has been reported.
levels.why: Sanctions are a main EU tool to pressure Russia over the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: The EU proposes a 22nd round of sanctions on Russia covering banks, soldiers and sport
levels.body:
The European Commission put forward its 22nd package of sanctions on Russia on 23 November. It would cut a further 60 Russian banks off the SWIFT payments network and crack down on crypto platforms.

Ursula von der Leyen revived a plan to ban Russian soldiers who have fought in Ukraine from entering the EU. A similar plan stalled in July after France and Italy voiced concerns over paperwork and legal burdens. The package would also exclude Russian teams and athletes under the Russian flag from sports events in the bloc. Von der Leyen said sport cannot be "a forum for propaganda activities".

All member states must agree, and Brussels wants a deal in December. Ukraine's sanctions envoy urged tougher steps, including on Rosatom and alumina. No approval has been reported.
levels.why: The package shows how the EU tries to raise pressure on Russia over the war.

levels.headline: The EU proposes new sanctions against Russian banks, soldiers and athletes
levels.body:
The European Commission has proposed a new set of sanctions on Russia. They are the 22nd since the war in Ukraine began in 2022. Sanctions are penalties on a country. The plan was put forward on 23 November.

It would cut 60 more Russian banks off SWIFT, the system banks use to send money abroad. It would also target crypto platforms. The Commission wants to ban Russian soldiers who have fought in Ukraine from entering the EU. A similar plan stalled in July because France and Italy had worries about the paperwork. Russian teams and athletes under the Russian flag would also be kept out of sports events in the EU.

Every member country must agree. The EU hopes for a deal in December. Ukraine wants even tougher steps.
levels.why: It shows how Europe tries to pressure Russia to end the war.

levels.headline: European countries want to put new penalties on Russia
levels.body:
Russia is fighting a war in Ukraine. Lots of European countries think it is wrong. They have decided to try to make it harder for Russia to keep fighting. One way is to give Russia penalties, which are called sanctions.

Now they want to add new ones. They want to stop some Russian banks from sending money to other countries. They want to stop Russian soldiers who fought in the war from visiting. They also want to stop Russian sports teams from taking part in games in Europe.

Before the new penalties can start, every country in the group has to say yes. That might take until December.
levels.why: It is a way for Europe to push Russia to stop the war.

levels.headline: European leaders want to give Russia a new set of penalties
levels.body:
Sometimes in the playground, one child hurts others. The teachers may then stop that child from joining in games for a while. That is a bit like sanctions.

Russia is fighting a war in Ukraine. Many European countries think this is wrong. They have given Russia penalties already. Now they want to add more. They want to stop some Russian banks from sending money abroad. They want to stop soldiers who fought in the war from visiting. They also want to stop Russian sports teams from taking part in games in Europe.

Before it can start, all the countries have to agree. They hope to do it before the winter holidays.
levels.why: It is a way for Europe to push Russia to stop the war.

levels.headline: European countries want to say no to some things Russia does
levels.body:
Imagine one child in your class keeps breaking an important rule. The other children might decide, as a group, to stop playing with that child for a while until things change. That is a bit like what some countries are doing now.

Russia is fighting a war in Ukraine. Many countries in Europe think this is wrong. They have decided to give Russia penalties, to try to make it stop.

Now they want to add more. Some Russian banks would be stopped from sending money to other countries. Some soldiers would not be allowed in. Sports teams would not be allowed to play in Europe.

All the countries have to say yes first. They hope to agree before the winter holidays.
levels.why: It is a way for countries to try to make Russia stop.

headline: Bank of Korea raises its base rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, a two-year high, and upgrades growth forecasts

terms.meaning: The central bank's main interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.
One hundredth of a percentage point.
South Korea's main stock market index.

levels.headline: Bank of Korea raises its base rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, a two-year high, and upgrades growth forecasts
levels.body:
The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.25% on 26 November, at its last policy meeting of the year. It is the third increase this year, after rises in July and August, and takes borrowing costs to a two-year high. The move was in line with economists' expectations.

The central bank lifted its 2026 growth forecast to 3.9% from 3.3%, and its 2027 forecast to 4.1% from 2.9%. It expects headline inflation to average 2.7% this year and 2.4% next year, both above its 2% target.

Governor Shin Hyun-song signalled that more rate rises were possible but gave no timeline. Gareth Leather of Capital Economics said there was reason to believe the tightening cycle was drawing to a close. The Kospi, South Korea's benchmark stock index, rose 1.88% after the decision.
levels.why: It shows central banks in Asia are still tightening to fight inflation, which affects global markets.

levels.headline: South Korea's central bank lifts rates to 3.25% and raises its growth forecasts
levels.body:
The Bank of Korea raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25% on 26 November, at its final meeting of the year. It is the third rise this year, after July and August, and the highest level in two years. Economists had expected it.

The bank raised its growth forecast for 2026 to 3.9% from 3.3%, and for 2027 to 4.1% from 2.9%. It expects inflation to average 2.7% this year and 2.4% next year, above its 2% target.

Governor Shin Hyun-song said more increases were possible, with no timeline. An analyst at Capital Economics said the tightening cycle might be nearing its end. The Kospi stock index rose 1.88% after the decision.
levels.why: It shows how central banks are still raising rates around the world.

levels.headline: South Korea raises interest rates to a two-year high of 3.25% as it expects stronger growth
levels.body:
South Korea's central bank, the Bank of Korea, raised its main interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25% on 26 November. It was the last meeting of the year. This is the third increase in 2026, after July and August. Interest rates are now at their highest for two years. Economists had expected the move.

The bank also expects the economy to grow faster. It now predicts growth of 3.9% this year, up from 3.3%, and 4.1% next year, up from 2.9%. It expects inflation, the rate at which prices rise, to be 2.7% this year, above its 2% target.

The governor said more rises were possible. South Korea's main stock index, the Kospi, rose 1.88% after the news.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make borrowing cost more and show how strong the economy is.

levels.headline: South Korea's central bank raises interest rates for the third time this year
levels.body:
The Bank of Korea, South Korea's central bank, raised its main interest rate on 26 November. The rate went up by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25%, the highest in two years. It is the third rise this year. Experts had expected it. A central bank changes interest rates to try to keep prices steady.

The bank thinks the economy will grow faster than it first said. It now expects growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% next year. It expects inflation, which is how fast prices rise, to be 2.7% this year. That is higher than its target of 2%.

The head of the bank, Shin Hyun-song, said further rises were possible. South Korea's main stock market index rose 1.88% after the news.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make loans cost more, but they aim to keep prices steady.

levels.headline: South Korea's central bank puts up interest rates again
levels.body:
South Korea is a country in Asia. It has a central bank, called the Bank of Korea. On 26 November, the bank put up its main interest rate to 3.25%. It is the third time this year. Interest rates are now the highest they have been for two years.

The bank does this to keep prices from going up too fast. If borrowing money costs more, people borrow and spend less. That helps to keep prices steady. Prices are rising by about 2.7% a year in South Korea. The bank would like it to be 2%.

The bank also thinks the country's economy will grow faster than it first guessed. The head of the bank said it may put up rates again. South Korea's main share index rose after the news.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make loans cost more, but help to keep prices steady.

The bank thinks the economy will grow faster than it said before. It now expects growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% next year. It expects inflation, the speed at which prices rise, to be 2.7% this year, which is above its 2% target.

levels.headline: South Korea's central bank raises the cost of borrowing again
levels.body:
South Korea is a country in Asia. It has a big bank that looks after the country's money, called a central bank. On 26 November, the bank raised its main interest rate to 3.25%. An interest rate is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. So now borrowing costs more. It is the third rise this year.

Why does the bank do this? Prices in the country are going up by about 2.7% a year. The bank wants that to be 2%. When it costs more to borrow, people spend less. That helps stop prices rising so fast.

The bank also says the country's economy is doing well. The head of the bank said more rises might come.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make loans cost more, but help to keep prices steady.

levels.headline: The bank in South Korea says borrowing money will cost more
levels.body:
South Korea is a country in Asia. It has a big bank that helps to look after all the money in the country. On 26 November, the bank said that borrowing money will now cost more. The extra money that you pay for a loan is called interest.

Why did the bank do it? Prices in shops there are going up a little faster than the bank likes. When borrowing costs more, people spend less. Then shop prices stop going up so fast.

It is the third time this year that the bank has done this.

The bank also said it thinks the country will be doing well next year. The head of the bank said that it may raise the cost of borrowing again.
levels.why: It may help to stop prices from going up too fast.

levels.headline: A bank in Asia makes borrowing cost a little more
levels.body:
Think of a piggy bank. A big bank is a bit like that, but for a whole country. South Korea has one. It looks after the country's money.

When someone borrows money, they have to pay back a little extra. That extra is called interest. On 26 November, South Korea's big bank said the extra will be a bit bigger. It is the third time this year.

Why? Prices in shops have been going up a bit too fast. If the extra for borrowing is bigger, people borrow less and spend less. Then prices stop going up so fast.

The bank also thinks the country is doing well. Grown-ups will keep watching.
levels.why: It helps to keep shop prices steady.

levels.headline: A big country bank says it costs a little more to borrow
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow a toy from a friend. When you give it back, you also give them a sweet to say thank you. That sweet is a bit like interest. It is the extra you pay when you borrow.

In South Korea, a faraway country, the big bank for the whole country has said the sweet will get a little bigger. This makes people think twice before borrowing. They might spend a little less.

Why do this? Prices in shops have been going up a bit fast. If people spend less, prices stop climbing so quickly.

The grown-ups at the bank think the country is doing well. They will keep watching to see if they need to change things again.
levels.why: It helps to keep shop prices steady.
